newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Terra Nova to build U.K. motor business.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Terra Nova to build U.K. motor business.

text.p: Terra Nova (Bermuda) Holdings Ltd plans to expand its new direct motor insurance business in the United Kingdom in 1997 amid expectations for a turnaround in pricing, a top company executive said.

Terra Nova chief executive William Bailey, in a recent telephone interview with Reuters, said the company began offering direct motor insurance through its Lloyd's managing agency at the start of this year as part of a reshaping of its business mix.

This strategic restructuring, which got underway in late 1994, will leave Bermuda-based Terra Nova much less vulnerable to losses from catastrophes as well as decrease its exposure to the highly competitive marine hull and energy sector, Bailey said.

"We have dramatically changed (the company's) form and its size from a predominantly reinsurance company in the property-casualty business with a marine insurance content to one that in 1997 will be roughly 50 percent reinsurance and 50 percent insurance," Bailey said.

The Terra Nova Group was created in December 1994 when Terra Nova Insurance Co, a 25-year-old London market, privately-owned reinsurer, was refinanced and became a subsidiary of Terra Nova (Bermuda) Holdings.
At the same time, the charter of a Bermuda company in run-off was acquired and renamed Terra Nova (Bermuda) Insurance Co.

Since then the company has posted strong growth in both premiums and earnings, Bailey said. In 1997, Bailey said, Terra Nova expects to have gross written premiums of $560 million, up from about $300 million in 1994.

In addition, he said he was comfortable with Wall Street's first quarter First Call consensus estimate of $0.59 a share, on more than 26 million average shares, compared with $0.56 a share, on 18.8 million average shares outstanding, in the year ago first quarter.
He said he also was comfortable with estimates of about $2.50 a share for 1997 compared with $2.26 a share in 1996.
The expansion in London as well as the decreased participation in the marine business will help propel earnings growth, Bailey said.
In 1997, marine hull will represent just about nine percent of Terra Nova's overall business, down from about 16 percent in 1995.
Meanwhile, Terra Nova plans to expand its aviation accident business and expects the U.K. direct motor business to represent about 13 percent of its overall business in 1997.

Terra Nova provides about 54 percent of the capacity for the syndicate that is underwriting the direct motor business, most of which is renewal business and therefore generally more profitable than new business, Bailey said.
The syndicate expects to write about 100 million stg this year, putting Terra Nova's share around 50 million stg or about $80 million, he said.
Terra Nova's expansion into the U.K. direct motor business underscores the company's increasing commitment to the London market as well, Bailey said.
In 1997, will commit 184 million stg of capacity at Lloyd's, which "puts us very far up the list of the largest capacity providers at Lloyds," Bailey said.
Several other Bermuda-based insurers, such as ACE Ltd and Mid Ocean Ltd, also have expanded their Lloyd's participation.
This diversification comes as insurers seek new markets to enter as they cut back their participation in their traditional businesses, where intense competition has driven down prices.
Some insurers, reluctant to write business at unattractive prices, also have begun to consider acquisitions as well to help spur growth and provide diversification.
However, even though ACE last year acquired Tempest Reinsurance Co Ltd, Bailey said he doubts that will herald a wave of consolidation in the Bermuda market.
"I don't find my confreres in that market walking around looking over their shoulders," Bailey said.
